entries.2b2440717fb78ccc32b537fc75c32fc2492bd83f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv97"/><title type="x-ms">Joel</title> <div sID="gen19992" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19993" type="x-p"/> <hi type="small-caps">We</hi> are altogether uncertain concerning the time when this prophet prophesied; it is probable that it was about the same time Amos prophesied, not for the reason that the rabbin give, "Because Amos begins his prophecy with that wherewith Joel concludes his, <hi type="italic">The Lord shall roar out of Zion,</hi>" but for the reason Dr. Lightfoot gives, "Because he speaks of the same judgments of locusts, and drought, and fire, that Amos laments, which is an intimation that they appeared about the same time, Amos in Israel and Joel in Judah. Hosea and Obadiah prophesied about the same time; and it appears that Amos prophesied in the days of Jeroboam, the second king of Israel, <reference osisRef="Amos.7.10">Amos vii. 10</reference>. God sent a variety of prophets, that they might strengthen the hands one of another, and that out of the mouth of two or three witnesses every word might be established. In this prophecy, I. The desolations made by hosts of noxious insects is described, <reference osisRef="Joel.1.1-Joel.2.11">ch. i. and part of ch. ii.</reference> II. The people are hereupon called to repentance, <reference osisRef="Joel.2.12-Joel.2.17">ch. ii.</reference> III. Promises are made of the return of mercy upon their repentance (<reference osisRef="Joel.2.18-Joel.2.32">ch. ii.</reference>), and promises of the pouring out of the Spirit in the latter days. IV. The cause of God's people is pleaded against their enemies, whom God would in due time reckon with (<reference osisRef="Joel.3.1-Joel.3.21">ch. iii.</reference>); and glorious things are spoken of the gospel—Jerusalem and of the prosperity and perpetuity of it. <div eID="gen19993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19994" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19995" type="x-p"/> This chapter is the description of a lamentable devastation made of the country of Judah by locusts and caterpillars. Some think that the prophet speaks of it as a thing to come and gives warning of it beforehand, as usually the prophets did of judgments coming. Others think that it was now present, and that his business was to affect the people with it and awaken them by it to repentance. I. It is spoken of as a judgment which there was no precedent of in former ages, <reference osisRef="Joel.1.1-Joel.1.7">ver. 1-7</reference>. II. All sorts of people sharing in the calamity are called upon to lament it, <reference osisRef="Joel.1.8-Joel.1.13">ver. 8-13</reference>. III. They are directed to look up to God in their lamentations, and to humble themselves before him, <reference osisRef="Joel.1.14-Joel.1.20">ver. 14-20</reference>. <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv97"/> <div eID="gen19995" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19994" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Threatenings of Judgment. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 720.)</title> <div sID="gen19996" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> that came to Joel the son of Pethuel. <hi type="super">2</hi> Hear this, ye old men, and give ear, all ye inhabitants of the land. Hath this been in your days, or even in the days of your fathers? <hi type="super">3</hi> Tell ye your children of it, and <hi type="italic">let</hi> your children <hi type="italic">tell</hi> their children, and their children another generation. <hi type="super">4</hi> That which the palmer-worm hath left hath the locust eaten; and that which the locust hath left hath the canker-worm eaten; and that which the canker-worm hath left hath the caterpillar eaten. <hi type="super">5</hi> Awake, ye drunkards, and weep; and howl, all ye drinkers of wine, because of the new wine; for it is cut off from your mouth. <hi type="super">6</hi> For a nation is come up upon my land, strong, and without number, whose teeth <hi type="italic">are</hi> the teeth of a lion, and he hath the cheek teeth of a great lion. <hi type="super">7</hi> He hath laid my vine waste, and barked my fig tree: he hath made it clean bare, and cast <hi type="italic">it</hi> away; the branches thereof are made white. <div eID="gen19996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19997" type="x-p"/> It is a foolish fancy which some of the Jews have, that this Joel the prophet was the same with that Joel who was the son of Samuel (<reference osisRef="1Sam.8.2">1 Sam. viii. 2</reference>); yet one of their rabbin very gravely undertakes to show why Samuel is here called <hi type="italic">Pethuel.</hi> This Joel was long after that. He here speaks of a sad and sore judgment which was now brought, or to be brought, upon Judah, for their sins. Observe, <div eID="gen19997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19998" type="x-p"/> I. The greatness of the judgment, expressed here in two things:—1. It was such as could not be paralleled in the ages that were past, in history, or in the memory of any living, <reference osisRef="Joel.1.2">v. 2</reference>. The <hi type="italic">old men</hi> are appealed to, who could remember what had happened long ago; nay, and <hi type="italic">all the inhabitants of the land</hi> are called on to testify, if they could any of them remember the like. Let them go further than any man's memory, and <hi type="italic">prepare themselves for the search of their fathers</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.8.8">Job viii. 8</reference>), and they would not find an account of the like in any record. Note, Those that outdo their predecessors in sin may justly expect to fall under greater and sorer judgments than any of their predecessors knew. 2. It was such as would not be forgotten in the ages to come (<reference osisRef="Joel.1.3">v. 3</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Tell you your children of it;</hi> let them know what dismal tokens of the wrath of God you have been under, that they make take warning, and may learn obedience by the things which you have suffered, for it is designed for warning to them also. Yea, let <hi type="italic">your children tell their children, and their children another generation;</hi> let them tell it not only as a strange thing, which may serve for matter of talk" (as such uncommon accidents are records in our almanacs—It is so long since the plague, and fire—so long since the great frost, and the great wind), "but let them tell it to <hi type="italic">teach their children</hi> to stand in awe of God and of his judgments, and to tremble before him." Note, We ought to transmit to posterity the memorial of God's judgments as well as of his mercies. <div eID="gen19998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19999" type="x-p"/> II. The judgment itself; it is an invasion of the country of Judea by a great army. Many interpreters both ancient and modern understand it of armies of men, the forces of the Assyrians, which, under Sennacherib, <hi type="italic">took all the defenced cities of Judah,</hi> and then, no doubt, made havoc of the country and destroyed the products of it: nay, some make the four sorts of animals here names (<reference osisRef="Joel.1.4">v. 4</reference>) to signify the four monarchies which, in their turns, were oppressive to the people of the Jews, one destroying what had escaped the fury of the other. Many of the Jewish expositors think it is a parabolic expression of the coming of enemies, and their multitude, to lay all waste. So the Chaldee paraphrast mentions these animals (<reference osisRef="Joel.1.4">v. 4</reference>); but afterwards (<reference osisRef="Joel.2.25">ch. ii. 25</reference>) puts instead of them, <hi type="italic">Nations, peoples, tongues, languages, potentates,</hi> and <hi type="italic">revenging kingdoms.</hi> But it seems much rather to be understood literally of armies of insects coming upon the land and eating up the fruits of it. Locusts were one of the plagues of Egypt. Of them it is said, There never were any like them, nor should be (<reference osisRef="Exod.10.14">Exod. x. 14</reference>), none such as those in Egypt, none such as these in Judah—none like those locusts for bigness, none like these for multitude and the mischief they did. The plague of locusts in Egypt lasted but for a few days; this seems to have continued for four years successively (as some think), because here are four sorts of insects mentioned (<reference osisRef="Joel.1.4">v. 4</reference>), one destroying what the other left; but others think they came all in one year. We are not told, in the history of the Old Testament, when this happened, but we are sure that no word of God fell to the ground; and, though a devastation by these insects is primarily intended here, yet it is expressed in such a language as is very applicable to the destruction of the country by a foreign enemy invading it, because, if the people were not humbled and reformed by that less judgment which devoured the land, God would send this greater upon them, which would devour the inhabitants; and by the description of that they are bidden to take it for a warning. If this nation of worms do not subdue them, another nation shall come to ruin them. Observe, 1. What these animals are that are sent against them—<hi type="italic">locusts</hi> and <hi type="italic">caterpillars, palmer-worms</hi> and <hi type="italic">canker-worms,</hi> <reference osisRef="Joel.1.4">v. 4</reference>. We cannot now describe how these differed one from another; they were all little insects, any one of them despicable, and which a man might easily crush with his foot or with his finger; but when they came in vast swarms, or shoals, they were very formidable and ate up all before them. Note, God is Lord of hosts, has all creatures at his command, and, when he pleases, can humble and mortify a proud and rebellious people by the weakest and most contemptible creatures. Man is said to be a worm; and by this it appears that he is <hi type="italic">less than a worm,</hi> for, when God pleases, worms are too hard for him, plunder his country, eat up that for which he laboured, destroy the forage, and cut off the subsistence of a potent nation. The weaker the instrument is that God employs the more is his power magnified. 2. What fury and force they came with. They are here called a <hi type="italic">nation</hi> (<reference osisRef="Joel.1.6">v. 6</reference>), because they are embodied, and act by consent, and as it were with a common design; for, though <hi type="italic">the locusts have no king, yet they go forth all of them by bands</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.30.27">Prov. xxx. 27</reference>), and it is there mentioned as an instance of their <hi type="italic">wisdom.</hi> It is prudence for those that are weak severally to unite and act jointly. They are <hi type="italic">strong,</hi> for they are <hi type="italic">without number.</hi> The <hi type="italic">small dust of the balance</hi> is light, and easily blown away, but a heap of dust is weighty; so a worm can do little (yet one worm served to destroy Jonah's gourd), but numbers of them can do wonders. They are said to have <hi type="italic">teeth of a lion,</hi> of a <hi type="italic">great lion,</hi> because of the great and terrible execution they do. Note, Locusts become as lions when they come armed with a divine commission. We read of the locusts out of the bottomless pit, that <hi type="italic">their teeth were as the teeth of lions,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.9.8">Rev. ix. 8</reference>. 3. What mischief they do. They <hi type="italic">eat up</hi> all before them (<reference osisRef="Joel.1.4">v. 4</reference>); what one leaves the other devours; they destroy not only the grass and corn, but the trees (<reference osisRef="Joel.1.7">v. 7</reference>): The <hi type="italic">vine is laid waste.</hi> There vermin eat the leaves which should be a shelter to the fruit while it ripens, and so that also perishes and comes to nothing. They eat the very bark of the fig-tree, and so kill it. Thus the <hi type="italic">fig-tree does not blossom,</hi> nor is there <hi type="italic">fruit in the vine.</hi> <div eID="gen19999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20000" type="x-p"/> III. A call to the drunkards to lament this judgment (<reference osisRef="Joel.1.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">Awake and weep, all you drinkers of wine.</hi> This intimates, 1. That they should suffer very sensibly by this calamity. It should touch them in a tender part; the <hi type="italic">new wine</hi> which they loved so well should be <hi type="italic">cut off from their mouth.</hi> Note, It is just with God to take away those comforts which are abused to luxury and excess, to <hi type="italic">recover</hi> the <hi type="italic">corn and wine</hi> which are <hi type="italic">prepared</hi> for Baal, which are made the food and fuel of a base lust. And to them judgments of that kind are most grievous. The more men place their happiness in the gratification of sense the more pressing temporal afflictions are upon them. The drinkers of water need not to care when the vine was laid waste; they could live as well without it as they had done; it was no trouble to the Nazarites. But the <hi type="italic">drinkers of wine</hi> will <hi type="italic">weep and howl.</hi> The more delights we make necessary to our satisfaction the more we expose ourselves to trouble and disappointment. 2. It intimates that they had been very senseless and stupid under the former tokens of God's displeasure; and therefore they are here called to <hi type="italic">awake and weep.</hi> Those that will not be roused out of their security by the word of God shall be roused by his rod; those that will not be startled by judgments at a distance shall be themselves arrested by them; and when they are going to partake of the forbidden fruit a prohibition of another nature shall come <hi type="italic">between the cup and the lip,</hi> and <hi type="italic">cut off the wine from their mouth.</hi>
entries.cb2956de4f35e8113643898016dd92b1bedd3157: <div eID="gen20000" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Threatenings of Judgment. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 720.)</title> <div sID="gen20001" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> Lament like a virgin girded with sackcloth for the husband of her youth. <hi type="super">9</hi> The meat offering and the drink offering is cut off from the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; the priests, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's ministers, mourn. <hi type="super">10</hi> The field is wasted, the land mourneth; for the corn is wasted: the new wine is dried up, the oil languisheth. <hi type="super">11</hi> Be ye ashamed, O ye husbandmen; howl, O ye vinedressers, for the wheat and for the barley; because the harvest of the field is perished. <hi type="super">12</hi> The vine is dried up, and the fig tree languisheth; the pomegranate tree, the palm tree also, and the apple tree, <hi type="italic">even</hi> all the trees of the field, are withered: because joy is withered away from the sons of men. <hi type="super">13</hi> Gird yourselves, and lament, ye priests: howl, ye ministers of the altar: come, lie all night in sackcloth, ye ministers of my God: for the meat offering and the drink offering is withholden from the house of your God. <div eID="gen20001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20002" type="x-p"/> The judgment is here described as very lamentable, and such as all sorts of people should share in; it shall not only rob the drunkards of their pleasure (if that were the worst of it, it might be the better borne), but it shall deprive others of their necessary subsistence, who are therefore called to lament (<reference osisRef="Joel.1.8">v. 8</reference>), as a virgin laments the death of her lover to whom she was espoused, but not completely married, yet so that he was in effect her husband, or as a young woman lately married, from whom the <hi type="italic">husband of her youth,</hi> her young husband, or the husband to whom she was married when she was young, is suddenly taken away by death. Between a new-married couple that are young, that married for love, and that are every way amiable and agreeable to each other, there is great fondness, and consequently great grief if either be taken away. Such lamentation shall there be for the loss of their corn and wine. Note, The more we are wedded to our creature-comforts that harder it is to part with them. See that parallel place, <reference osisRef="Isa.32.10-Isa.32.12">Isa. xxxii. 10-12</reference>. Two sorts of people are here brought in, as concerned to lament this devastation, countrymen and clergymen. <div eID="gen20002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20003" type="x-p"/> I. Let the husbandmen and vine-dressers lament, <reference osisRef="Joel.1.11">v. 11</reference>. Let them be ashamed of the care and pains they have taken about their vineyards, for it will be all labour lost, and they shall gain no advantage by it; they shall see the fruit of their labour eaten up before their eyes, and shall not be able to save any of it. Note, Those who labour only <hi type="italic">for the meat that perishes</hi> will, sooner or later, be ashamed of their labour. The <hi type="italic">vine-dressers</hi> will then express their extreme grief by <hi type="italic">howling,</hi> when they see their vineyards stripped of leaves and fruit, and the vines withered, so that nothing is to be had or hoped for from them, wherewith they might pay their rent and maintain their families. The destruction is particularly described here: <hi type="italic">The field is laid waste</hi> (<reference osisRef="Joel.1.10">v. 10</reference>).; all is consumed that is produced; <hi type="italic">the land mourns;</hi> the ground has a melancholy aspect, and looks ruefully; all the inhabitants of the land are in tears for what they have lost, are in fear of perishing for want, <reference osisRef="Isa.24.4">Isa. xxiv. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.4.28">Jer. iv. 28</reference>. "The <hi type="italic">corn,</hi> the bread-corn, which is the staff of life, is <hi type="italic">wasted;</hi> the <hi type="italic">new wine,</hi> which should be brought into the cellars for a supply when the old is drunk, is <hi type="italic">dried up,</hi> is <hi type="italic">ashamed</hi> of having promised so fair what it is not now able to perform; the oil <hi type="italic">languishes,</hi> or is <hi type="italic">diminished,</hi> because (as the Chaldee renders it) <hi type="italic">the olives have fallen off.</hi>" The people were not thankful to God as they should have been for the <hi type="italic">bread that strengthens man's heart,</hi> the <hi type="italic">wine</hi> that <hi type="italic">makes glad the heart,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">oil that makes the face to shine</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.14-Ps.104.15">Ps. civ. 14, 15</reference>); and therefore they are justly brought to lament the loss and want of them, of all the products of the earth, which God had given either for necessity or for delight (this is repeated, <reference osisRef="Joel.1.11-Joel.1.12">v. 11, 12</reference>)—the <hi type="italic">wheat and barley,</hi> the two principal grains bread was then made of, wheat for the rich and barley for the poor, so that the rich and poor meet together in the calamity. The trees are destroyed, not only the <hi type="italic">vine and the fig-tree</hi> (as before, <reference osisRef="Joel.1.7">v. 7</reference>), which were more useful and necessary, but other trees also that were for delight—the <hi type="italic">pomegranate, palm-tree,</hi> and <hi type="italic">apple-tree,</hi> yea, all the <hi type="italic">trees of the field,</hi> as well as those of the orchard, timber-trees as well as fruit-trees. In short, all <hi type="italic">the harvest of the field has perished,</hi> <reference osisRef="Joel.1.11">v. 11</reference>. And by this means <hi type="italic">joy has withered away from the children of men</hi> (<reference osisRef="Joel.1.11">v. 11</reference>); the <hi type="italic">joy of harvest,</hi> which is used to express great and general joy, has come to nothing, is turned into shame, is turned into lamentation. Note, The perishing of the harvest is the withering of the joy of the children of men. Those that place their happiness in the delights of the sense, when they are deprived of them, or in any way disturbed in the enjoyment of them, lose all their joy; whereas the children of God, who look upon the pleasures of sense with holy indifference and contempt, and know what it is to make God their hearts' delight, can rejoice in him as the <hi type="italic">God of their salvation</hi> even when the <hi type="italic">fig-tree does not blossom;</hi> spiritual joy is so far from withering then, that it flourishes more than ever, <reference osisRef="Hab.3.17-Hab.3.18">Hab. iii. 17, 18</reference>. Let us see here, 1. What perishing uncertain things all our creature-comforts are. We can never be sure of the continuance of them. Here the heavens had given their rains in due season, the earth had yielded her strength, and, when the appointed weeks of harvest were at hand, they saw no reason to doubt but that they should have a very plentiful crop; yet then they are invaded by these unthought-of enemies, that lay all waste, and not by fire and sword. It is our wisdom not to lay up our treasure in those things which are liable to so many untoward accidents. 2. See what need we have to live in continual dependence upon God and his providence, for our own hands are not sufficient for us. When we see the <hi type="italic">full corn in the ear,</hi> and think we are sure of it—nay, when we have <hi type="italic">brought it home,</hi> if <hi type="italic">he blow upon it,</hi> nay, if he do not bless it, we are not likely to have any good of it. 3. See what ruinous work sin makes. A paradise is turned into a wilderness, a fruitful land, the most fruitful land upon earth, <hi type="italic">into barrenness,</hi> for the <hi type="italic">iniquity of those that dwelt therein.</hi> <div eID="gen20003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20004" type="x-p"/> II. Let the priests, the Lord's ministers, lament, for they share deeply in the calamity: <hi type="italic">Gird yourselves</hi> with sackcloth (<reference osisRef="Joel.1.13">v. 13</reference>); nay, they <hi type="italic">do mourn,</hi> <reference osisRef="Joel.1.9">v. 9</reference>. Observe, The priests are called the <hi type="italic">ministers of the altar,</hi> for on that they attended, and the <hi type="italic">ministers of the Lord</hi> (of <hi type="italic">my God,</hi> says the prophet), for in attending on the altar they served him, did is work, and did him honour. Note, Those that are employed in holy things are therein God's ministers, and on him they attend. The ministers of the altar used to rejoice before the Lord, and to spend their time very much in singing; but now they must <hi type="italic">lament and howl,</hi> for the <hi type="italic">meat-offering</hi> and <hi type="italic">drink-offering</hi> were <hi type="italic">cut off from the house of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Joel.1.9">v. 9</reference>), and the same again (<reference osisRef="Joel.1.13">v. 13</reference>), <hi type="italic">from the house of your God.</hi> "He is your God in a particular manner; you are in a nearer relation to him than other Israelites are; and therefore it is expected that you should be more concerned than others for that which is a hindrance to the service of his sanctuary." It is intimated, 1. That the people, as long as they had the fruits of the earth brought in in their season, presented to the Lord his dues out of them, and brought the offerings to the altar and tithes to those that served at the altar. Note, A people may be filling up the measure of their iniquity apace, and yet may keep up a course of external performances in religion. 2. That, when the meat and drink failed, the meat-offering and drink-offering failed of course; and this was the sorest instance of the calamity. Note, As far as any public trouble is an obstruction to the course of religion it is to be upon that account, more than any other, sadly lamented, especially by the priests, the Lord's ministers. As far as poverty occasions the decay of piety and the neglect of divine offices, and starves the cause of religion among a people, it is indeed a sore judgment. When the famine prevailed God could not have his sacrifices, nor could the priests have their maintenance; and therefore let <hi type="italic">the Lord's ministers mourn.</hi>
entries.d3cc6706f775b073b6a0c659f830ca5f07a52531: <div eID="gen20004" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Threatenings of Judgment; A Proclamation for a Fast. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 720.)</title> <div sID="gen20005" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> Sanctify ye a fast, call a solemn assembly, gather the elders <hi type="italic">and</hi> all the inhabitants of the land <hi type="italic">into</hi> the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God, and cry unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , <hi type="super">15</hi> Alas for the day! for the day of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> at hand, and as a destruction from the Almighty shall it come. <hi type="super">16</hi> Is not the meat cut off before our eyes, <hi type="italic">yea,</hi> joy and gladness from the house of our God? <hi type="super">17</hi> The seed is rotten under their clods, the garners are laid desolate, the barns are broken down; for the corn is withered. <hi type="super">18</hi> How do the beasts groan! the herds of cattle are perplexed, because they have no pasture; yea, the flocks of sheep are made desolate. <hi type="super">19</hi> <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , to thee will I cry: for the fire hath devoured the pastures of the wilderness, and the flame hath burned all the trees of the field. <hi type="super">20</hi> The beasts of the field cry also unto thee: for the rivers of waters are dried up, and the fire hath devoured the pastures of the wilderness. <div eID="gen20005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20006" type="x-p"/> We have observed abundance of tears shed for the destruction of the fruits of the earth by the locusts; now here we have those tears turned into the right channel, that of repentance and humiliation before God. The judgment was very heavy, and here they are directed to own the hand of God in it, his <hi type="italic">mighty hand,</hi> and to <hi type="italic">humble themselves</hi> under it. Here is, <div eID="gen20006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20007" type="x-p"/> I. A proclamation issued out for a general fast. The priests are ordered to appoint one; they must not only mourn themselves, but they must call upon others to mourn too: "<hi type="italic">Sanctify a fast;</hi> let some time be set apart from all worldly business to be spent in the exercises of religion, in the expressions of repentance and other extraordinary instances of devotion." Note, Under public judgments there ought to be public humiliations; for by them the <hi type="italic">Lord God calls to weeping and mourning.</hi> With all the marks of sorrow and shame sin must be confessed and bewailed, the righteous of God must be acknowledged, and his favour implored. Observe what is to be done by a nation at such a time. 1. A day is to be appointed for this purpose, a <hi type="italic">day of restraint</hi> (so the margin reads it), a day in which people must be restrained from their other ordinary business (that they may more closely attend God's service), and from all bodily refreshments; for, 2. It must be a <hi type="italic">fast,</hi> a religious abstaining from meat and drink, further than is of absolute necessity. The king of Nineveh appointed a fast, in which they were to <hi type="italic">taste nothing,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jonah.3.7">Jonah iii. 7</reference>. Hereby we own ourselves unworthy of our necessary food, and that we have forfeited it and deserve to be wholly deprived of it, we punish ourselves and mortify the body, which has been the occasion of sin, we keep it in a frame fit to serve the soul in serving God, and, by the appetite's craving food, the desires of the soul towards that which is better than life, and all the supports of it, are excited. This was in a special manner seasonable now that God was depriving them of their <hi type="italic">meat and drink;</hi> for hereby they accommodated themselves to the affliction they were under. When God says, <hi type="italic">You shall fast,</hi> it is time to say, <hi type="italic">We will fast.</hi> 3. There must be a solemn assembly. The <hi type="italic">elders</hi> and the <hi type="italic">people,</hi> magistrates and subjects, must be <hi type="italic">gathered together,</hi> even <hi type="italic">all the inhabitants of the land,</hi> that God might be honoured by their public humiliations, that they might thereby take the more shame to themselves, and that they might excite and stir up one another to the religious duties of the day. All had contributed to the national guilt, all shared in the national calamity, and therefore they must all join in the professions of repentance. 4. They must come together in the temple, <hi type="italic">the house of the Lord</hi> their <hi type="italic">God,</hi> because that was the house of prayer, and there they might be hope to meet with God because it was the place which he had <hi type="italic">chosen to put his name there,</hi> there they might hope to speed because it was a type of Christ and his mediation. Thus they interested themselves in Solomon's prayer for the acceptance of all the requests that should be put up in or towards this house, in which their present case was particularly mentioned. <reference osisRef="1Kgs.7.37">1 Kings vii. 37</reference>, <hi type="italic">If there be locust, if there be caterpillar.</hi> 5. They must <hi type="italic">sanctify</hi> this fast, must observe it in a religious manner, with sincere devotion. What is a fast worth if it be not sanctified? 6. They must <hi type="italic">cry unto the Lord.</hi> To him they must make their complaint and offer up their supplication. When we cry in our affliction we must <hi type="italic">cry to the Lord;</hi> this is <hi type="italic">fasting to him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.7.5">Zech. vii. 5</reference>. <div eID="gen20007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20008" type="x-p"/> II. Some considerations suggested to induce them to proclaim this fast and to observe it strictly. <div eID="gen20008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20009" type="x-p"/> 1. God was beginning a controversy with them. It is time to <hi type="italic">cry unto the Lord,</hi> for <hi type="italic">the day of the Lord is at hand,</hi> <reference osisRef="Joel.1.15">v. 15</reference>. Either they mean the continuance and consequences of this present judgment which they now saw but breaking in upon them, or some greater judgments which this was but a preface to. However it be, this they are taught to make the matter of their lamentation: <hi type="italic">Alas, for the day! for the day of the Lord is at hand.</hi> Therefore <hi type="italic">cry to God.</hi> For, (1.) "The day of his judgment is very near, it is <hi type="italic">at hand;</hi> it <hi type="italic">will not slumber,</hi> and therefore you should not. It is time to fast and pray, for you have but a little time to turn yourselves in." (2.) It will be very terrible; there is no escaping it, no resisting it: <hi type="italic">As a destruction from the Almighty shall it come.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Isa.13.6">Isa. xiii. 6</reference>. It is not a correction, but a destruction; and it comes from the hand, not of a weak creature, but <hi type="italic">of the Almighty;</hi> and <hi type="italic">who knows</hi> (nay, who does not know) <hi type="italic">the power of his anger?</hi> Whither should we go with our cries but to him from whom the judgment we dread comes? There is no fleeing from him but by fleeing to him, no escaping destruction from the Almighty but by making our submission and supplication to the Almighty; this is <hi type="italic">taking hold on his strength, that we may make peace,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.27.5">Isa. xxvii. 5</reference>. <div eID="gen20009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20010" type="x-p"/> 2. They saw themselves already under the tokens of his displeasure. It is time to fast and pray, for their distress is very great, <reference osisRef="Joel.1.16">v. 16</reference>. (1.) Let them look into their own houses, and was no plenty there, as used to be. Those who kept a good table were now obliged to retrench: <hi type="italic">Is not the meat cut off before our eyes?</hi> If, when God's hand is lifted up, men <hi type="italic">will not see,</hi> when his hand is laid on <hi type="italic">they shall see.</hi> Is not the meat many a time cut off before our eyes? Let us then labour for that spiritual meat which is not before our eyes, and which cannot be cut off. (2.) Let them look into God's house, and see the effects of the judgment there; joy and gladness were <hi type="italic">cut off from the house of God.</hi> Note, The house of our God is the proper place of joy and gladness; when David goes to the <hi type="italic">altar of God,</hi> it is to God <hi type="italic">my exceeding joy;</hi> but when <hi type="italic">joy and gladness</hi> are <hi type="italic">cut off from God's house,</hi> either by corruption of holy things or the persecution of holy persons, when serious godly decays and love waxes cold, then it time to cry to the Lord, time to cry, <hi type="italic">Alas!</hi> <div eID="gen20010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20011" type="x-p"/> 3. The prophet returns to describe the grievousness of the calamity, in some particulars of it. Corn and cattle are the husbandman's staple commodities; now here he is deprived of both. (1.) The caterpillars have devoured the corn, <reference osisRef="Joel.1.17">v. 17</reference>. The <hi type="italic">garners,</hi> which they used to fill with corn, <hi type="italic">are laid desolate,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the barns broken down,</hi> because <hi type="italic">the corn has withered,</hi> and the owners think it not worth while to be at the charge of repairing them when they have nothing to put in them, nor are likely to have any thing; for <hi type="italic">the seed it rotten under the clods,</hi> either through too much rain or (which was the more common case in Canaan) for want of rain, or perhaps some insects under ground ate it up. When one crop fails the husband man hopes the next may make it up; but here they despair of that, the seedness being as bad as the harvest. (2.) The cattle perish too for want of grass (<reference osisRef="Joel.1.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">How do the beasts groan!</hi> This the prophet takes notice of, that the people might be affected with it and lay to heart the judgment. The groans of the cattle should soften their hard and impenitent hearts. <hi type="italic">The herds of cattle,</hi> the large cattle (black cattle we call them), <hi type="italic">are perplexed;</hi> nay, even <hi type="italic">the flocks of sheep,</hi> which will live upon a common and be content with very short grass, <hi type="italic">are made desolate.</hi> See here the inferior creatures suffering for our transgression, and groaning under the double burden of being serviceable to the sin of man and subject to the curse of God for it. <hi type="italic">Cursed is the ground for thy sake.</hi> <div eID="gen20011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20012" type="x-p"/> III. The prophet stirs them up to cry to God, with the consideration of the examples given them for it. <div eID="gen20012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20013" type="x-p"/> 1. His own example (<reference osisRef="Joel.1.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">O Lord! to thee will I cry.</hi> He would not put them upon doing that which he would not resolve to do himself; nay, whether they would do it or no, he would. Note, If God's ministers cannot prevail to affect others with the discoveries of divine wrath, yet they ought to be themselves affected with them; if they cannot bring others to cry to God, yet they themselves be much in prayer. In time of trouble we must not only pray, but cry, must be fervent and importunate in prayer; and to God, from whom both the destruction is and the salvation must be, ought our cry to be always directed. That which engaged him <hi type="italic">to cry to God</hi> was, not so much any personal affliction, as the national calamity: The <hi type="italic">fire has devoured the pastures of the wilderness,</hi> which seems to be meant of some parching scorching heat of the sun, which was as fire to the fruits of the earth; it consumed them all. Note, When God <hi type="italic">calls to contend by fire</hi> it concerns those that have any interest in heaven to cry mightily to him for relief. See <reference osisRef="Num.11.2">Num. xi. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.7.4-Amos.7.5">Amos vii. 4, 5</reference>. <div eID="gen20013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20014" type="x-p"/> 2. The example of the inferior creatures: "<hi type="italic">The beasts of the field</hi> do not only <hi type="italic">groan,</hi> but <hi type="italic">cry unto thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Joel.1.20">v. 20</reference>. They appeal to thy pity, according to their capacity, and as if, though they are not capable of a rational and revealed religion, yet they had something of dependence upon God by natural instinct." At least, when they groan by reason of their calamity, he is pleased to interpret it as if they cried to him; much more will he put a favourable construction upon the groanings of his own children, though sometimes so feeble that they <hi type="italic">cannot be uttered,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.8.26">Rom. viii. 26</reference>. The beasts are here said to <hi type="italic">cry unto God,</hi> as from him the <hi type="italic">lions seek their meat</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.21">Ps. civ. 21</reference>) and the young <hi type="italic">ravens,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.38.41">Job xxxviii. 41</reference>. The complaints of the brute-creatures here are for want of water (<hi type="italic">The rivers are dried up,</hi> through the excessive heat), and for want of grass, for the <hi type="italic">fire has devoured the pastures of the wilderness.</hi> And what better are those than beasts who never cry to God but for corn and wine, and complain of nothing but the want of delight of sense? Yet their crying to God in those cases shames the stupidity of those who cry not to God in any case.  <chapter eID="Joel.1"/> <div eID="gen20014" type="x-p"/>

entries.14d0ce4c33e5f1b526972341d9623c69bd0025e1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12435"/><title type="x-IS">INTRODUCTION</title> <div sID="gen22824" type="x-p"/> Joel (meaning "one to whom Jehovah is God," that is, worshipper of Jehovah) seems to have belonged to Judah, as no reference occurs to Israel; whereas he speaks of Jerusalem, the temple, the priests, and the ceremonies, as if he were intimately familiar with them (compare <reference osisRef="Joel.1.14">Joe 1:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.15">2:1, 15</reference>, 32; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.1">3:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.16">2, 6, 16</reference>, 17, 20, 21). His predictions were probably delivered in the early days of Joash 870-865 B.C.; for no reference is made in them to the Babylonian, Assyrian, or even the Syrian invasion; and the only enemies mentioned are the Philistines, Phoenicians, Edomites, and Egyptians (<reference osisRef="Joel.3.4">Joe 3:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joel.3.19">19</reference>). Had he lived after Joash, he would doubtless have mentioned the Syrians among the enemies whom he enumerates since they took Jerusalem and carried off immense spoil to Damascus (<reference osisRef="2Chr.24.23">2Ch 24:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.24">24</reference>). No idolatry is mentioned; and the temple services, the priesthood, and other institutions of the theocracy, are represented as flourishing. This all answers to the state of things under the high priesthood of Jehoiada, through whom Joash had been placed on the throne and who lived in the early years of Joash (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.11.17">2Ki 11:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.11.18">18</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.12.2-2Kgs.12.16">12:2-16</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.4-2Chr.24.14">2Ch 24:4-14</reference>). He was the son of Pethuel.<div eID="gen22824" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22823" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22825" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">The first chapter describes the desolation caused by an inroad of locusts--</hi>one of the instruments of divine judgment mentioned by Moses (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.38">De 28:38</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.28.39">39</reference>) and by Solomon (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.37">1Ki 8:37</reference>). The second chapter (<reference osisRef="Joel.2.1-Joel.2.11">Joe 2:1-11</reference>): the appearance of them, under images of a hostile army suggesting that the locusts were symbols and forerunners of a more terrible scourge, namely, foreign enemies who would consume all before them. (The absence of mention of personal injury to the inhabitants is not a just objection to the figurative interpretation; for the figure is consistent throughout in attributing to the locusts only injury to vegetation, thereby injuring indirectly man and beast). <reference osisRef="Joel.2.12-Joel.2.17">Joe 2:12-17</reference>: exhortation to repentance, the result of which will be: God will deliver His people, the former and latter rains shall return to fertilize their desolated lands, and these shall be the pledge of the spiritual outpouring of grace beginning with Judah, and thence extending to "all flesh." <reference osisRef="Joel.2.18-Joel.3.21">Joe 2:18-3:21</reference>: God's judgments on Judah's enemies, whereas Judah shall be established for ever.<div eID="gen22825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22826" type="x-p"/> Joel's style is pre-eminently pure. It is characterized by smoothness and fluency in the rhythms, roundness in the sentences, and regularity in the parallelisms. With the strength of Micah it combines the tenderness of Jeremiah, the vividness of Nahum, and the sublimity of Isaiah. As a specimen of his style take the second chapter wherein the terrible aspect of the locusts, their rapidity, irresistible progress, noisy din, and instinct-taught power of marshalling their forces for their career of devastation, are painted with graphic reality.<div eID="gen22826" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">CHAPTER 1</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Joel.1.1-Joel.1.20">Joe 1:1-20</reference>. The Desolate Aspect of the Country through the Plague of Locusts; the People Admonished to Offer Solemn Prayers in the Temple; for This Calamity Is the Earnest of a Still Heavier One.</title> <div sID="gen22827" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12435"/><hi type="bold">1. Joel--</hi>meaning, "Jehovah is God."<div eID="gen22827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22828" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">son of Pethuel--</hi>to distinguish Joel the prophet from others of the name. Persons of eminence also were noted by adding the father's name. <div eID="gen22828" type="x-p"/>
entries.edd1c563e26ba2a5871956fe012592e193a6f031: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12436"/><div sID="gen22829" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12436"/>2-3. A spirited introduction calling attention.<div eID="gen22829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22830" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">old men--</hi>the best judges in question concerning the past (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.7">De 32:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.32.7">Job 32:7</reference>).<div eID="gen22830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22831" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Hath this been, &c.--</hi>that is, Hath any so grievous a calamity as this ever been before? No such plague of locusts had been since the ones in Egypt. <reference osisRef="Exod.10.14">Ex 10:14</reference> is not at variance with this verse, which refers to Judea, in which Joel says there had been no such devastation before. <div eID="gen22831" type="x-p"/>
entries.3646d2e29ac9c0f20e9fa1abc523a546665bfb09: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12438"/><div sID="gen22833" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12438"/>4. This verse states the subject on which he afterwards expands. Four species or stages of locusts, rather than four different insects, are meant (compare <reference osisRef="Lev.11.22">Le 11:22</reference>). Literally, (1) the gnawing locust; (2) the swarming locust; (3) the licking locust; (4) the consuming locust; forming a climax to the most destructive kind. The last is often three inches long, and the two antennæ, each an inch long. The two hinder of its six feet are larger than the rest, adapting it for leaping. The first "kind" is that of the locust, having just emerged from the egg in spring, and without wings. The second is when at the end of spring, still in their first skin, the locusts put forth little ones without legs or wings. The third, when after their third casting of the old skin, they get small wings, which enable them to leap the better, but not to fly. Being unable to go away till their wings are matured, they devour all before them, grass, shrubs, and bark of trees: translated "rough caterpillars" (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.27">Jr 51:27</reference>). The fourth kind, the matured winged locusts (see on <reference osisRef="Nah.3.16">Na 3:16</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Joel.2.25">Joe 2:25</reference> they are enumerated in the reverse order, where the restoration of the devastations caused by them is promised. The Hebrews make the first species refer to Assyria and Babylon; the second species, to Medo-Persia; the third, to Greco-Macedonia and Antiochus Epiphanes; the fourth, to the Romans. Though the primary reference be to literal locusts, the Holy Spirit doubtless had in view the successive empires which assailed Judea, each worse than its predecessor, Rome being the climax. <div eID="gen22833" type="x-p"/>
entries.7c03b40899d4ea0fca549f75bc6f0bb6cb870356: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12439"/><div sID="gen22834" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12439"/><hi type="bold">5. Awake--</hi>out of your ordinary state of drunken stupor, to realize the cutting off from you of your favorite drink. Even the drunkards (from a Hebrew root, "any strong drink") shall be forced to "howl," though usually laughing in the midst of the greatest national calamities, so palpably and universally shall the calamity affect all.<div eID="gen22834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22835" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wine ... new wine--</hi>"New" or "fresh wine," in Hebrew, is the unfermented, and therefore unintoxicating, sweet juice extracted by pressure from grapes or other fruit, as pomegranates (<reference osisRef="Song.8.2">So 8:2</reference>). "Wine" is the produce of the grape alone, and is intoxicating (see on <reference osisRef="Joel.1.10">Joe 1:10</reference>). <div eID="gen22835" type="x-p"/>
entries.570726184e61fc56c37b05bc1bf1f487f798a277: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12440"/><div sID="gen22836" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12440"/><hi type="bold">6. nation--</hi>applied to the locusts, rather than "people" (<reference osisRef="Prov.30.25">Pr 30:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.30.26">26</reference>), to mark not only their numbers, but also their savage hostility; and also to prepare the mind of the hearer for the transition to the figurative locusts in the second chapter, namely, the "nation" or Gentile foe coming against Judea (compare <reference osisRef="Joel.2.2">Joe 2:2</reference>).<div eID="gen22836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22837" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my land--</hi>that is, Jehovah's; which never would have been so devastated were I not pleased to inflict punishment (<reference osisRef="Joel.2.18">Joe 2:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.14.25">Is 14:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.16.18">Jr 16:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.5">Eze 36:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.38.16">38:16</reference>).<div eID="gen22837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22838" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">strong--</hi>as irresistibly sweeping away before its compact body the fruits of man's industry.<div eID="gen22838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22839" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">without number--</hi>so <reference osisRef="Judg.6.5">Jud 6:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.7.12">7:12</reference>, "like grasshoppers (or "locusts") for multitude" (<reference osisRef="Jer.46.23">Jr 46:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Nah.3.15">Na 3:15</reference>).<div eID="gen22839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22840" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">teeth ... lion--</hi>that is, the locusts are as destructive as a lion; there is no vegetation that can resist their bite (compare <reference osisRef="Rev.9.8">Re 9:8</reference>). Pliny says "they gnaw even the doors of houses." <div eID="gen22840" type="x-p"/>
entries.25b2ad4de7c4cf26bb2543e8554a930f97f520cc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12441"/><div sID="gen22841" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12441"/><hi type="bold">7. barked--</hi>Bochart, with the Septuagint and Syriac, translates, from an Arabic root, "hath broken," namely, the topmost shoots, which locusts most feed on. Calvin supports English Version.<div eID="gen22841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22842" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my vine ... my fig tree--</hi>being in "My land," that is, Jehovah's (<reference osisRef="Joel.1.6">Joe 1:6</reference>). As to the vine-abounding nature of ancient Palestine, see <reference osisRef="Num.13.23">Nu 13:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.13.24">24</reference>.<div eID="gen22842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22843" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cast it away--</hi>down to the ground.<div eID="gen22843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22844" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">branches ... white--</hi>both from the bark being stripped off (<reference osisRef="Gen.30.37">Ge 30:37</reference>), and from the branches drying up through the trunk, both bark and wood being eaten up below by the locusts. <div eID="gen22844" type="x-p"/>
entries.c0a1e0b2fae89b9a2242f8f98326829c383b0d9d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12442"/><div sID="gen22845" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12442"/><hi type="bold">8. Lament--</hi>O "my land" (<reference osisRef="Joel.1.6">Joe 1:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.24.4">Is 24:4</reference>).<div eID="gen22845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22846" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">virgin ... for the husband--</hi>A virgin betrothed was regarded as married (<reference osisRef="Deut.22.23">De 22:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.1.19">Mt 1:19</reference>). The Hebrew for "husband" is "lord" or "possessor," the husband being considered the master of the wife in the East.<div eID="gen22846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22847" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of her youth--</hi>when the affections are strongest and when sorrow at bereavement is consequently keenest. Suggesting the thought of what Zion's grief ought to be for her separation from Jehovah, the betrothed husband of her early days (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.2">Jr 2:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.8">Eze 16:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.2.7">Ho 2:7</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Prov.2.17">Pr 2:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.4">Jr 3:4</reference>). <div eID="gen22847" type="x-p"/>
entries.5968e6ba65984e9eba4f5e1780dd594c7f67c960: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12443"/><div sID="gen22848" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12443"/>9. The greatest sorrow to the mind of a religious Jew, and what ought to impress the whole nation with a sense of God's displeasure, is the cessation of the usual temple-worship.<div eID="gen22848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22849" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">meat offering--</hi>Hebrew, mincha; "meat" not in the English sense "flesh," but the unbloody offering made of flour, oil, and frankincense. As it and the drink offering or libation poured out accompanied every sacrificial flesh offering, the latter is included, though not specified, as being also "cut off," owing to there being no food left for man or beast.<div eID="gen22849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22850" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">priests ... mourn--</hi>not for their own loss of sacrificial perquisites (<reference osisRef="Num.18.8-Num.18.15">Nu 18:8-15</reference>), but because they can no longer offer the appointed offerings to Jehovah, to whom they minister. <div eID="gen22850" type="x-p"/>
entries.06085e0cd74bfbca6fa8baedc902da8db2318f1e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12444"/><div sID="gen22851" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12444"/><hi type="bold">10. field ... land--</hi>differing in that "field" means the open, unenclosed country; "land," the rich red soil (from a root "to be red") fit for cultivation. Thus, "a man of the field," in Hebrew, is a "hunter"; a "man of the ground" or "land," an "agriculturist" (<reference osisRef="Gen.25.27">Ge 25:27</reference>). "Field" and "land" are here personified.<div eID="gen22851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22852" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">new wine--</hi>from a Hebrew root implying that it takes possession of the brain, so that a man is not master of himself. So the Arabic term is from a root "to hold captive." It is already fermented, and so intoxicating, unlike the sweet fresh wine, in <reference osisRef="Joel.1.5">Joe 1:5</reference>, called also "new wine," though a different Hebrew word. It and "the oil" stand for the vine and the olive tree, from which the "wine" and "oil" are obtained (<reference osisRef="Joel.1.12">Joe 1:12</reference>).<div eID="gen22852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22853" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dried up--</hi>not "ashamed," as Margin, as is proved by the parallelism to "languisheth," that is, droopeth. <div eID="gen22853" type="x-p"/>
entries.50b275df9ddee36fab1412324a5201aa18ad6e36: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12445"/><div sID="gen22854" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12445"/><hi type="bold">11. Be ... ashamed--</hi>that is, Ye shall have the shame of disappointment on account of the failure of "the wheat" and "barley ... harvest."<div eID="gen22854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22855" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">howl ... vine dressers--</hi>The semicolon should follow, as it is the "husbandmen" who are to be "ashamed ... for the wheat." The reason for the "vine dressers" being called to "howl" does not come till <reference osisRef="Joel.1.12">Joe 1:12</reference>, "The vine is dried up." <div eID="gen22855" type="x-p"/>
entries.470c026cd9b9b2d5986584940dd083a3cd798e93: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12446"/><div sID="gen22856" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12446"/><hi type="bold">12. pomegranate--</hi>a tree straight in the stem growing twenty feet high; the fruit is of the size of an orange, with blood-red colored pulp.<div eID="gen22856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22857" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">palm tree--</hi>The dates of Palestine were famous. The palm is the symbol of Judea on coins under the Roman emperor Vespasian. It often grows a hundred feet high.<div eID="gen22857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22858" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">apple tree--</hi>The Hebrew is generic, including the orange, lemon, and pear tree.<div eID="gen22858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22859" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">joy is withered away--</hi>such as is felt in the harvest and the vintage seasons (<reference osisRef="Ps.4.7">Psa 4:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.9.3">Is 9:3</reference>). <div eID="gen22859" type="x-p"/>
entries.f5ed92a25c69c94135910a1fd5033e01ee67b79f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12447"/><div sID="gen22860" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12447"/><hi type="bold">13. Gird yourselves--</hi>namely, with sackcloth; as in <reference osisRef="Isa.32.11">Is 32:11</reference>, the ellipsis is supplied (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.4.8">Jr 4:8</reference>).<div eID="gen22860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22861" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lament, ye priests--</hi>as it is your duty to set the example to others; also as the guilt was greater, and a greater scandal was occasioned, by your sin to the cause of God.<div eID="gen22861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22862" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">come--</hi>the Septuagint, "enter" the house of God (compare <reference osisRef="Joel.1.14">Joe 1:14</reference>).<div eID="gen22862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22863" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lie all night in sackcloth--</hi>so Ahab (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.21.27">1Ki 21:27</reference>).<div eID="gen22863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22864" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ministers of my God--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.13">1Co 9:13</reference>). Joel claims authority for his doctrine; it is in God's name and by His mission I speak to you. <div eID="gen22864" type="x-p"/>
entries.82451233da44a6118e380bc59ed6d2e72fb6fa15: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12448"/><div sID="gen22865" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12448"/><hi type="bold">14. Sanctify ... a fast--</hi>Appoint a solemn fast.<div eID="gen22865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22866" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">solemn assembly--</hi>literally, a "day of restraint" or cessation from work, so that all might give themselves to supplication (<reference osisRef="Joel.2.15">Joe 2:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.16">16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.5">1Sa 7:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.3-2Chr.20.13">2Ch 20:3-13</reference>).<div eID="gen22866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22867" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">elders--</hi>The contrast to "children" (<reference osisRef="Joel.2.16">Joe 2:16</reference>) requires age to be intended, though probably elders in office are included. Being the people's leaders in guilt, they ought to be their leaders also in repentance. <div eID="gen22867" type="x-p"/>
entries.af2d681c05d65156ad28942ba7881bc399df26b9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12449"/><div sID="gen22868" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12449"/><hi type="bold">15. day of the Lord--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Joel.2.1">Joe 2:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.11">11</reference>); that is, the day of His anger (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.9">Is 13:9</reference>; Ob 15; <reference osisRef="Zeph.1.7">Zep 1:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.15">15</reference>). It will be a foretaste of the coming day of the Lord as Judge of all men, whence it receives the same name. Here the transition begins from the plague of locusts to the worse calamities (<reference osisRef="Joel.2.1-Joel.2.11">Joe 2:1-11</reference>) from invading armies about to come on Judea, of which the locusts were the prelude. <div eID="gen22868" type="x-p"/>
entries.55aa9d369ff98f8874996a11333a618f8581ad15: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12450"/><div sID="gen22869" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12450"/>16. Compare <reference osisRef="Joel.1.9">Joe 1:9</reference>, and latter part of <reference osisRef="Joel.1.12">Joe 1:12</reference>.<div eID="gen22869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22870" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">joy--</hi>which prevailed at the annual feasts, as also in the ordinary sacrificial offerings, of which the offerers ate before the Lord with gladness and thanksgivings (<reference osisRef="Deut.12.6">De 12:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.7.12">7, 12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.16.11">16:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.14.15">14, 15</reference>). <div eID="gen22870" type="x-p"/>
entries.b76118de67bacb03270a2b4345757744c6eb6040: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12451"/><div sID="gen22871" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12451"/><hi type="bold">17. is rotten--</hi>"is dried up," "vanishes away," from an Arabic root [Maurer]. "Seed," literally, "grains." The drought causes the seeds to lose all their vitality and moisture.<div eID="gen22871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22872" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">garners--</hi>granaries; generally underground, and divided into separate receptacles for the different kinds of grain. <div eID="gen22872" type="x-p"/>
entries.a4609d807818165d9786a955b5b27133688ea525: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12452"/><div sID="gen22873" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12452"/><hi type="bold">18. cattle ... perplexed--</hi>implying the restless gestures of the dumb beasts in their inability to find food. There is a tacit contrast between the sense of the brute creation and the insensibility of the people.<div eID="gen22873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22874" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">yea, the ... sheep--</hi>Even the sheep, which are content with less rich pasturage, cannot find food.<div eID="gen22874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22875" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">are made desolate--</hi>literally, "suffer punishment." The innocent brute shares the "punishment" of guilty man (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.29">Ex 12:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jonah.3.7">Jon 3:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jonah.4.11">4:11</reference>). <div eID="gen22875" type="x-p"/>
entries.caff0f5990c4d9187f0a506b67d3c222d2149b40: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12453"/><div sID="gen22876" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12453"/><hi type="bold">19. to thee will I cry--</hi>Joel here interposes, As this people is insensible to shame or fear and will not hear, I will leave them and address myself directly to Thee (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.15.5">Is 15:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.23.9">Jr 23:9</reference>).<div eID="gen22876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22877" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fire--</hi>that is, the parching heat.<div eID="gen22877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22878" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pastures--</hi>"grassy places"; from a Hebrew root "to be pleasant." Such places would be selected for "habitations" (Margin). But the English Version rendering is better than Margin. <div eID="gen22878" type="x-p"/>
entries.bc50cf7ad25d2aeb53a945d5e5d8af2b0fe0f58a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12454"/><div sID="gen22879" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12454"/><hi type="bold">20. beasts ... cry ... unto thee--</hi>that is, look up to heaven with heads lifted up, as if their only expectation was from God (<reference osisRef="Job.38.41">Job 38:41</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.104.21">Psa 104:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.145.15">145:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.147.9">147:9</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Ps.42.1">Psa 42:1</reference>). They tacitly reprove the deadness of the Jews for not even now invoking God. <chapter eID="Joel.1"/>

entries.09273b0c29d82fb2e6c68667b61b4a6ffff9d2ad: <div eID="gen34028" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction to the Book of the Prophet Joel</title> <div sID="gen34029" type="x-p"/> Joel, the son of Pethuel, the second of the twelve minor prophets, was, as is said, of the tribe of Reuben, and city of Bethoran; or rather Betharan, for Bethoran was on this side Jordan, in the tribe of Ephraim, and Betharan was on the other side of the river, in the tribe of Reuben. Joel prophesied in the kingdom of Judah; and it is the opinion of some critics that he did not appear there till after the removal of the ten tribes and the destruction of the kingdom of Israel. We do not know distinctly the year wherein he began to prophesy, nor that in which he died. He speaks of a great famine, and an inundation of locusts, which ravaged Judea; but as these are evils not uncommon in that country, and all sorts of events have not been registered in history, we can infer nothing from thence towards fixing the particular period of Joel's prophecy. <div eID="gen34029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34030" type="x-p"/> St. Jerome, followed by many others, both ancients and moderns, believed Joel to have been contemporary with Hosea, according to this rule laid down by him, that when there is no certain proof of the time wherein any prophet lived, we are to be directed in our conjectures by the time of the preceding prophet, whose epoch is better known. But this rule is not always certain, and should not hinder us from following another system, if we have good reason for doing so. The Hebrews maintain that Joel prophesied under Manasseh; and as collateral circumstances seem to preponderate in favor of this hypothesis, it has been accordingly followed in the margin. Under the idea of an enemy's army, the prophet represents a cloud of locusts, which in his time fell upon Judea, and caused great desolation. This, together with the caterpillars, and the drought, brought a terrible famine upon the land. God, being moved with the calamities and prayers of his people, scattered the locusts, and the wind blew them into the sea. These misfortunes were succeeded by plenty and fertility. After this, the prophet foretold the day of the Lord, and the vengeance he was to exercise in the valley of Jezreel. He speaks of the teacher of righteousness, whom God was to send; and of the Holy Spirit, which was to descend upon all flesh. He says that Jerusalem will be inhabited for ever; that salvation will come out from thence; and that whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved. All this relates to the new covenant, and the time of the Messiah. See Calmet. <div eID="gen34030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34031" type="x-p"/> Bishop Lowth observes that "the style of Joel differs much from that of Hosea; but, though of a different kind, is equally poetical. It is elegant, perspicuous, clear, diffusive, and flowing; and, at the same time, very sublime, nervous, and animated. He displays the whole power of poetic description in the first and second chapters; and, at the same time, his fondness for metaphors, comparisons, and allegories; nor is the connection of his subjects less remarkable than the graces of his diction. It is not to be denied that in some places he is very obscure; which every attentive reader will perceive, especially in the end of this prophecy." Prael. xxi.; and see Dodd. The two first chapters are inimitably beautiful; and the language, in force, and often in sound, well adapted to the subject. See the note on <reference osisRef="Joe.1.1">Joe 1:1</reference> (note). <div eID="gen34031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34032" type="x-p"/> This and the beginning of the next chapter contain a double prophecy, applicable in its primary sense to a plague of locusts which was to devour the land, and to be accompanied with a severe drought and famine; and in its secondary sense it denotes the Chaldean invasion. Both senses must be admitted: for some of the expressions will apply only to the dearth by insects; others to the desolation by war. The contexture of both is beautiful and well conducted. In this chapter the distress of every order of people is strongly painted; and not only does the face of nature languish when the God of nature is displeased, vv. 1-19; but the very beasts of the field, by a bold figure, are represented as supplicating God in their distress, and reproaching the stupidity of man, <reference osisRef="Joe.1.20">Joe 1:20</reference>. <div eID="gen34032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34033" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen34033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34034" type="x-p"/> The word of the Lord that came to Joel - See the introduction for some account of this prophet, whose history is very obscure. Bishop Newcome thinks that he prophesied while the kingdom of Judah subsisted, and refers to <reference osisRef="Joe.2.1">Joe 2:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joe.2.15">Joe 2:15</reference>, (see also <reference osisRef="Joe.1.14">Joe 1:14</reference> (note), and the note there), but not long before its subversion as his words, <reference osisRef="Joe.3.1">Joe 3:1</reference>, seem to imply that its captivity was approaching. See <reference osisRef="2Kgs.21.10-2Kgs.21.15">2Kgs 21:10-15</reference>. He therefore favors the conjecture of Drusius, that this prophet lived under Manasseh, and before his conversion, <reference osisRef="2Chr.33.13">2Chr 33:13</reference>; that is, some time from before Christ 697 to (suppose) 660.
entries.b7f6f3bc1e9faa0bd6d9ad9c2ed346261e373d3b: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen34034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34035" type="x-p"/> Ye old men - Instead of הזקנים hazzekenim old men, a few MSS. have הכהנים haccohanim, ye priests, but improperly. <div eID="gen34035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34036" type="x-p"/> Hath this been in your days - He begins very abruptly; and before he proposes his subject, excites attention and alarm by intimating that he is about to announce disastrous events, such as the oldest man among them has never seen, nor any of them learnt from the histories of ancient times.
entries.16cd84ce0af39ee73d0c7aff761a4bf5ab7244af: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen34036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34037" type="x-p"/> Tell ye your children of it - To heighten the effect, he still conceals the subject, and informs them that it is such as should be handed down from father to son through all generations.
entries.061967d34f2a5d980c1572dc6e45728e0db7d4e0: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen34037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34038" type="x-p"/> That which the palmerworm hath left - Here he begins to open his message, and the words he chooses show that he is going to announce a devastation of the land by locusts, and a famine consequent on their depredations. What the different insects may be which he specifies is not easy to determine. I shall give the words of the original, with their etymology. <div eID="gen34038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34039" type="x-p"/> The palmerworm, גזם gazam, from the same root, to cut short; probably the caterpillar, or some such blight, from its cutting the leaves of the trees into pieces for its nourishment. <div eID="gen34039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34040" type="x-p"/> The locust, ארבה arbeh, from רבה rabah, to multiply, from the immense increase and multitude of this insect. <div eID="gen34040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34041" type="x-p"/> Cankerworm, ילק yelek, from לק lak, to lick or lap with the tongue; the reference is uncertain. <div eID="gen34041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34042" type="x-p"/> Caterpillar, חסיל chasil, from חסל chasal, to consume, to eat up, the consumer. Bishop Newcome translates the first grasshopper; the second, locust; the third, devouring locust; and the fourth, consuming locust. After all that has been said by interpreters concerning these four animals, I am fully of opinion that the arbeh, or locust himself, is the gazam, the yelek, and the chasil and that these different names are used here by the prophet to point out the locust in its different states, or progress from embryo to full growth. See the note on <reference osisRef="Joe.2.2">Joe 2:2</reference> (note).
entries.ad72e8070e8dda17d44ddc0063ba81b12bd0fa2a: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen34042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34043" type="x-p"/> Awake, ye drunkards - The general destruction of vegetation by these devouring creatures has totally prevented both harvest and vintage; so that there shall not be wine even for necessary uses, much less for the purposes of debauchery. It is well known that the ruin among the vines by locusts prevents the vintage for several years after.
entries.8890b7fda9ef8783bc838e502029e01084b686cd: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen34043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34044" type="x-p"/> A nation is come up upon my land - That real locusts are intended there can be little doubt; but it is thought that this may be a double prophecy, and that the destruction by the Chaldeans may also be intended, and that the four kinds of locusts mentioned above may mean the four several attacks made on Judea by them. The first in the last year of Nabonassar, (father of Nebuchadnezzar), which was the third of Jehoiakim; the second when Jehoiakim was taken prisoner in the eleventh year of his reign; the third in the ninth year of Zedekiah and the fourth three years after, when Jerusalem was destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar. Others say that they mean four powers which have been enemies of the Jews: <div eID="gen34044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34045" type="x-p"/> 1. The palmerworm, the Assyrians and Chaldeans. <div eID="gen34045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34046" type="x-p"/> 2. The locust, the Persians and Medes. <div eID="gen34046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34047" type="x-p"/> 3. The cankerworm, the Greeks, and particularly Antiochus Epiphanes. <div eID="gen34047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34048" type="x-p"/> 4. The caterpillar, the Romans. <div eID="gen34048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34049" type="x-p"/> Others make them four kings; Tiglath-pileser, Shalmaneser, Sennacherib, and Nebuchadnezzar. But of such similitudes there is no end; and the best of them is arbitrary and precarious.
entries.00d67e4b64f21a59d09e759c64b31a0b2d1ece33: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen34049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34050" type="x-p"/> He hath laid my vine waste - The locusts have eaten off both leaves and bark. חשף חשפה chasoph chasaphah, he hath made it clean bare; שדד שדה suddad sadeh, the field is laid waste, <reference osisRef="Joe.1.10">Joe 1:10</reference>; and כשד משדי kesod mishshaddai, a destruction from the Almighty, <reference osisRef="Joe.1.15">Joe 1:15</reference>; are all paronomasias in which this prophet seems to delight.
entries.baf4416f3278847664a17f3d9247458e90aaf635: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen34050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34051" type="x-p"/> Lament like a virgin - for the husband of her youth - Virgin is a very improper version here. The original is בתולה bethulah, which signifies a young woman or bride not a virgin, the proper Hebrew for which is עלמה almah. See the notes on <reference osisRef="Isa.7.14">Isa 7:14</reference> (note), and <reference osisRef="Mat.1.23">Mat 1:23</reference> (note).
entries.0d230a6b1c1de2699a037cff7008fb8591b9d0b9: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen34051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34052" type="x-p"/> The meat-offering and the drink-offering is cut off - The crops and the vines being destroyed by the locusts, thee total devastation in plants, trees, corn, etc., is referred to and described with a striking variety of expression in this and the following verses.
entries.def1d1000d199fead62db7ca14c5cd6a954c47a2: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen34052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34053" type="x-p"/> The vine is dried up - Dr. Shaw observes that in Barbary, in the month of June, the locusts collect themselves into compact bodies a furlong or more square, and march on, eating up every thing that is green or juicy, and letting nothing escape them, whether vegetables or trees. <div eID="gen34053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34054" type="x-p"/> They destroy the pomegranate, the palm, the apple, (תפוח tappuach, the citron tree), the vine, the fig, and every tree of the field. See the note on <reference osisRef="Joe.2.2">Joe 2:2</reference> (note).
entries.a3da193c3e3ce85a9b32016a65246abccfe165ef: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen34054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34055" type="x-p"/> Call a solemn assembly - עצרה atsarah signifies a time of restraint, as the margin has it. The clause should be translated - consecrate a fast, proclaim a time of restraint; that is, of total abstinence from food, and from all secular employment. All the elders of the land and the representatives of the people were to be collected at the temple to cry unto the Lord, to confess their sins, and pray for mercy. The temple was not yet destroyed. This prophecy was delivered before the captivity of Judah.
entries.fc50c6eb60f35df411e8629a36f759f80785dc68: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen34055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34056" type="x-p"/> Alas for the day! - The Syriac repeats this, the Vulgate, Septuagint, and Arabic, thrice: "Alas, alas, alas, for the day!" <div eID="gen34056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34057" type="x-p"/> As a destruction from the Almighty - The destruction that is now coming is no ordinary calamity; it is as a signal judgment immediately inflicted by the Almighty.
entries.beba91f4eaa93a0704f3053b25e7c1400f37fd3d: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen34057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34058" type="x-p"/> The seed is rotten under their clods - When the sprout was cut off as low as possible by the locusts, there was no farther germination. The seed rotted away.
entries.a354fbc623aa0eb7a6edc7331d27662d7e9fc354: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen34058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34059" type="x-p"/> How do the beasts groan! - I really think that the neighing of horses, or braying of asses, is wonderfully expressed by the sound of the original: מה נאנחה בהמה mah Neenchah behemah, how do the horses neigh! how do the asses bray! בהמה behemah is a collective name for all domestic cattle, and those used in husbandry. <div eID="gen34059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34060" type="x-p"/> Cattle are perplexed - They are looking everywhere, and wandering about to find some grass, and know not which way to run.
entries.ef0c35854de29c20eedb3ea5a57661a84ba80d38: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen34060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34061" type="x-p"/> O Lord, to thee will I cry - Let this calamity come as it may, we have sinned, and should humble ourselves before God; and it is such a calamity as God alone can remove, therefore unto him must we cry. <div eID="gen34061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34062" type="x-p"/> The fire hath devoured the pastures - This may either refer to a drought, or to the effects of the locusts; as the ground, after they have passed over it, everywhere appears as if a sheet of flame had not only scorched, but consumed every thing.
entries.2d46acb317b2356f06c7aee21d8053b7672fc8e6: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen34062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34063" type="x-p"/> The beasts of the field cry also unto thee - Even the cattle, wild and tame, are represented as supplicating God to have mercy upon them, and send them provender!
