               <ns0:head>CHAP. I.</ns0:head>
               <ns0:p n="1">1 THE word of the LORD that came to <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Since this Preface is word for word the same with that of <ns0:hi>Hosea, chap.</ns0:hi> 1. <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 1. see it there explained.</ns0:note> Joel <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Supposed to be of the Posterity of <ns0:hi>Reuben,</ns0:hi> therefore could not be (as the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> suppose) <ns0:hi>Samuel</ns0:hi>'s Son, nor will his time fit to 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 5.4, 8. but of what Tribe soever, we know he came from God, and with his authority, and is so cited by the Apostle, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 2.16.</ns0:note> the son of Pethuel <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">More of this man I know not, and 'tis possible he might be, as the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> suppose, very eminent, because he is named, how<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ever 'tis an honour to be reported a Prophets Father. The time of his Prophesying, though not demonstrable, is with greatest probability laid about the latter end of <ns0:hi>Ieroboam</ns0:hi> the second his Reign over <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> and in the dayes of <ns0:hi>Vzziah</ns0:hi> over <ns0:hi>Iudah.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="2">2 Hear this <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">He is about to report a very wonderful occurrence, and desires all to consider it, mark it well, and tell me what you know.</ns0:note>, ye old men <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">The oldest among you, who can remember things done in your dayes, when you were young, some scores of years past.</ns0:note>, and give ear all ye inhabitants <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">It is an appeal to all that may possibly know more then others, and remember better then others can.</ns0:note> of the land <ns0:hi>g:</ns0:hi> Hath this been in your dayes <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Did you per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sonally ever know the like?</ns0:note>, or even in the days of your fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLunhyphen" />thers <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Did your Fathers ever tell you of such a thing happening in their dayes? was there ever such a thing known among them? Have you ever heard them speak of it?</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">3 Tell ye <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Declare it very particularly, or record it, write it as in a book, that your children may know it, and the memory of it may be perpetuated, for as it was a very wonderful and unusual thing; so it was for to mind us of the cause of it, and what it taught, or should have taught them and us.</ns0:note> your children of it, and <ns0:hi>let</ns0:hi> your children <ns0:hi>tell</ns0:hi> their children, and their children a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nother generation.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>the re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sidue of the palmer-worm.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> That which the palmer-worm hath left, hath the locust eaten; and that which the locust hath left, hath the canker-worm eaten; and that which the canker-worm hath left, hath the cater<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pillar eaten.<ns0:note place="bottom">Four sorts of Insects pernicious to all sorts of Trees, Corn and Herbs, are here mentioned, which did succeed each other, and devouted all that might be a future support to the <ns0:hi>Iewes,</ns0:hi> whence ensued a grievous famine for four years together, say the <ns0:hi>Iewish</ns0:hi> Interpreters, though there is no cogent reason in what they mention for proof hereof. These insects might in the same year succeed each other, the one as is usual might come sooner, the rest successively, each in its season, and so spoil the springing of all things, which they did (I do believe) really, and though these might be Emblems of some future de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vastation, yet it seems most agreeable to reason, and the Con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />text, that there should really have been such caterpillars, and other vermine, and that they did devour all that was green; and though this is no where else mentioned, as I remember, in the sacred History, yet it is likely 'twas done, as here told, and as so done was a figure of some greater devastation made by Forreign Powers, as by <ns0:hi>Tiglath-Pileser, Salmaneser, Sennacherib</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Nebuchadnezzar.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:160" />5 Awake <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Great drinkers of intoxicating liquors are apt to sleep, and be secure, the Prophet doth therefore here call to them, as to sleepers, and by one apt word expresseth a double duty, vigi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lance of mind, as well as of the body, so may this be paral<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lel'd with <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 13.11. 1 <ns0:hi>Thes.</ns0:hi> 5.6. 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 5.8. or <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 5.14.</ns0:note> ye drunkards <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Riotous livers, such as <ns0:hi>Prov</ns0:hi> 23.30, 31, 32. and <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 5.11, 12. whose life is nothing but a continued feasting with choicest Wines, and in excess, such as <ns0:hi>Amos</ns0:hi> 6.4, 5, 6. de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />scribeth.</ns0:note> and weep, and howl <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Lament your condition with sober tears, for the sorrowes coming upon you are just matter of weeping, nor will an ordinary degree of weeping suffice. Cry out, and howl like men surprized with unsupportable miseries, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 13.6 and 14.32. and 15.2.</ns0:note> all ye drinkers of wine <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Who offend by an inordinate use of Wine, for it is not to be understood of every one that drinketh Wine, but of such as before are called drunkards, who are in love with Wine.</ns0:note>, because of the new wine <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Which is sweet and pleasing to the taste, and no doubt drank without stint or measure by men of that Age, against which <ns0:hi>Ioel</ns0:hi> Prophesieth.</ns0:note>, for it is cut off from your mouth <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Suddenly cut off, even when you are ready to drink it, and totally all cut off by these devouring vermin; which as 'twas a Narrative of what was al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ready done, refers to that waste and famine by the locusts, as 'tis Allegorical and Predictive, 'twill be more dreadfully fulfil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led when the enemies of <ns0:hi>Iudah</ns0:hi> shall destroy all.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 For a nation <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">An innumerable multitude of locusts and catterpil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lars, called a Nation here, as <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi> calls the Conies and the Ant, <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 30.25, 26. A prognostick of a very numerous and mighty Nation, that ere long will invade <ns0:hi>Iudah.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> is come up <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Or sud<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />denly will come</ns0:note> upon my land <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">upon <ns0:hi>Canaan</ns0:hi> which God calls his land, or more particularly the two Tribes, <ns0:hi>Iudea</ns0:hi> strictly taken,</ns0:note>, strong <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Migh<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty in power, and undaunted in courage, if you refer it to the <ns0:hi>Assyrian</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Babylonians</ns0:hi>; if to those vermin, they are, though each weak by it self, yet in those multitudes which come, strong enough, and irresistible, and shall do Gods work, that is, waste the Land, and devour all before them.</ns0:note>, and without number <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Not simply numberless, but in such multitudes none of you shall be able to recount them.</ns0:note>, whose teeth <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> the teeth of a lyon <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">A strong Lyon, of the middle Age, that hath Whelps, and hunts the prey for them.</ns0:note>, and he hath the cheek teeth of a great lyon <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Which is old, and the more fierce and terrible in his looks, no way les<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sened in his strength, and that preys for his young ones, now what waste such Lyons make, such these Locusts will make, such <ns0:hi>Assyrians</ns0:hi> will make.</ns0:note>.<ns0:note place="bottom">This verse countenanceth their conjecture, who take the lo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />custs and vermin to be Emblematical in part as well as literal; for it seems not very suitable, to call their teeth, teeth of a Lyon.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 He <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">That Nation of locusts <ns0:hi>verse</ns0:hi> 6. both literally and mistically understood.</ns0:note> hath laid my vine waste <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Made it a desolation, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> most desolate, which is more particularly declared in what followeth.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. laid <ns0:hi>my fig-tree for a barking.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> barked <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Peel'd off the bark, which is certain destruction to the Tree.</ns0:note> my fig tree: he hath made it clean bare <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Eat of all the rind, and green bark, and left the body of both Vine and Fig-tree bare and stript.</ns0:note>, and cast <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> away <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">As vermin cast out of their mouth, the chewings of what they spoil, so here,</ns0:note>, the branches <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">all the branches of both Vine and Fig-tree are by these devouring ver<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />min made white, all their green being eaten off; so miserably desolate will the enemy signified by these locusts, make <ns0:hi>Iu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dah,</ns0:hi> Gods Vine.</ns0:note> there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />of are made white.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 ¶ Lament <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">This is minatory, and threatens calamitous times shall come, as well as directive, what to do when they are come, when God calls for weeping, we must not rejoyce.</ns0:note> like a virgin <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">This tells us to whom the Prophet directs this part of his Ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mon, 'tis to those who amidst the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> were like chast and modest Virgins, whose heart was fixed on one, her own, her chosen beloved Husband.</ns0:note> girded with sackcloth <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">In deep mournings the people of those Countries did use sackcloth in their mourning habit, and wore it girded close to their skin.</ns0:note> for the husband of her youth <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Either married to her in youth, or espoused to her, but snatcht away from her by an untimely death, which she doth most bitterly lament.</ns0:note>.<ns0:note place="bottom">The vicious and wicked among the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> were alarmed and threatned in the former part of the Chapter; Now the Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phet bespeaks the good and Godly among them to prepare for mournful times.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 The meat-offering <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Which by divine appointment was to be of fine Flower, Oyl and Frankincense, as <ns0:hi>Lev.</ns0:hi> 2.1. <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> and 6.14. <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> This meat-offer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing was necessary to every Sacrifice offered under the Law; so that without the Mincha, or meat-offering, the Sacrifice was maimed and illegal.</ns0:note> and the drink-offering <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Required daily, as appears <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 29.40, 41. and <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 28.8. a fourth part of a hin of wine, for one lamb, <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 28.7.</ns0:note> is cut off <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">By the destruction of the vines, by the locusts forementioned, all that wine (out of which they ought to offer the drink-offering) did fail.</ns0:note> from the house of the LORD <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">It was to be pour<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed out if Wine, and part of the meat-offering was to be burnt on the Altar, so both were disposed according to the Law, in the house of the Lord.</ns0:note>; the priests <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Sons of <ns0:hi>Aaron,</ns0:hi> with the <ns0:hi>Levites,</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> the LORDS ministers <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">who did serve the Lord in the services of the Temple.</ns0:note> mourn <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Grieve inwardly, and express it by outward signs, these had more cause then others to mourn, for as they had equal cause with others in respect to God, whose service hereby failed, so the Priests, in respect to their private gain and maintenance had more cause to mourn, their provision was by this means shortened.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 The field is wasted <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">The soil that was wont to be fat and fruitful, and did shout with fruits, now lyeth waste, horrid to look upon, and such as promises no fruit, the famine in their houses, and the ceasing of the Sacrifices in the house of God, is like to be perpetuated.</ns0:note>, the land mourneth <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">The inhabitants of the Land by an usual figure, here called the Land.</ns0:note>, for the corn is wasted <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">The Wheat and Barley, their bread corn is eaten up in its greenness by these devouring locusts, whether in the letter by vermine, or in the figure by the <ns0:hi>Babylonians.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>: the new wine is <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 span">
                        <ns0:desc>〈…〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> dryed up <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">The word may as well be rendered is <ns0:hi>ashamed,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>confounded,</ns0:hi> 'tis then a figurative expression, which this Prophet useth, <ns0:hi>verse</ns0:hi> 12.17. in the last of which 'tis rendered, <ns0:hi>withered,</ns0:hi> if you retain as well you may, our Version, it plainly tells us, the heats and drought with them was so great, that the Vines were withered, and all their hopes of new wine by this means cut off.</ns0:note>, the oyl <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">The Olive-Trees as the Vines fade too, and promise very little Oyl.</ns0:note> languisheth <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Neither able to send sap from the root to maintain its verdure, nor to put forth berries, or to bring them to maturity. Now as these words declare what barrenness was now upon the land; so 'tis a plain account of the reason why the Priests are called to mourn, and why the meat-offering and drink-offering are <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> off, these must cease when that ceaseth, which made them up Corn, Wine and Oyl.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 Be ye ashamed, O ye husbandmen <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Some read it assertively, the Husbandmen are ashamed, and as to matter of fact, 'tis true, they were ashamed, but the Im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />perative Mood, or by way of Exhortation it better will suit the Context; They are now called upon to blush, repent and search into the cause of this barrenness, and loss of their labour in plowing, sowing and manuring their Tillage, the Prophet aims at this principally, to bring them, as well as the Priests to Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pentance.</ns0:note>: howl, O ye vine-dressers <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">A sort of men so well known with that people, as Gardiners are with us, men whose work was to plant, water, prune and manage Vineyards, and whose labour (unless for sin blasted) did usually succeed to a great increase.</ns0:note>, for the wheat, and for the barley; because the harvest of the field is pe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rished <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Your sins have brought upon you this woful scarcity, your harvest in which you expected your labours and cares should be recom<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />penced is perished, quite destroy'd, as the word imports. This is just cause why you O Husbandmen should lament and farther enquire why God is so displeased with you.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 The vine is dryed up <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">See <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 10. <ns0:hi>let.</ns0:hi> u.</ns0:note>, and the fig-tree <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">A Tree well known, and the fruit of it was usually a great advantage, and benefit to the peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple of those Countries.</ns0:note> languisheth, the pomegranate-tree <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">A pleasant tree as appears <ns0:hi>Cant.</ns0:hi> 4.13. and 7.12. and its fruit lovely, therefore fit for ornaments about the pillars of the Temple. These in the common drought and by locusts have lost their beauty, and fail the hopes of him that planted them.</ns0:note>, the palm-tree <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Of great beauty in the height, and uni<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />formity of its growth, and that doth rise under the weight which would depress it, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 92.12. with these <ns0:hi>Ezekiels</ns0:hi> Temple was adorned, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 40.16, 22, 26. with the branches of these, tri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />umphant shews were also made, but these are wither'd and dry.</ns0:note> also, and the apple-tree <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">The fruit whereof was very useful, and did ordinarily well recompence the care of the Planter, but now as other trees fail them.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> all the trees of the field <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">None so hardy and able to bear unkind seasons, but are now destroyed by the judgments of God in drought and lo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />custs.</ns0:note> are withered <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Not as in <ns0:hi>Autumn,</ns0:hi> when the leaf falleth, but because the root fails is either dead or dying.</ns0:note>, because <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Or therefore, or sure<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly, for the particle here used is oftentimes assertive, not causal.</ns0:note> joy is withered away from the sons of men.<ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">All mirth and livelyness of men is blasted with this dismal blast upon their labours and hopes, they cannot rejoyce who foresee they shall be, nay, are already pincht with want and famine.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:160" />13 Gird <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Bind your mourning sackcloth close to you with a girdle, that it may be more troublesome to the flesh, for though in <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 'tis only gird, the phrase is well known in the Scripture, on these occasions, to include sackcloth, as what is girded on the mourner, and <ns0:hi>verse</ns0:hi> 8. sackcloth is expresly mentioned, and in many other places, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 15.3. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 4.8. <ns0:hi>Lam.</ns0:hi> 2.10. <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 7.18. and 27.31.</ns0:note> your selves, and lament <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Weep bitterly as they do who mourn for the dead, lament over your dead joyes, let it be a hearty grief, as that of <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> for <ns0:hi>Sarah, Gen.</ns0:hi> 23.2. of <ns0:hi>Iacob</ns0:hi>'s children and friends sorrowing for his death, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 50.10. or of <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi> lamenting their brave Judge, 1 <ns0:hi>Sam</ns0:hi>: 28.3.</ns0:note>, ye priests <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">That you may be example to others, and because they had, as ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />served <ns0:hi>verse</ns0:hi> 9. a double cause to mourn, one more then the rest of the people.</ns0:note>: howl <ns0:note n="†" place="bottom">See <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 5. <ns0:hi>let.</ns0:hi> n.</ns0:note> ye ministers of the altar <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Verse</ns0:hi> 9. <ns0:hi>let.</ns0:hi> p. They were the Lords Ministers, now Ministers of the Altar, they served the Lord in the things of the Altar.</ns0:note>: come, lie all night <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">The case needs a conti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nued fasting, weeping and supplication in the most humble po<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sture, and with all the tokens of an afflicted spirit. The Priests should above others mourn, if they mourn in the day, the Priests should mourn night and day.</ns0:note> in sackcloth, ye ministers of my God <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Who having sent me to speak to you in his name, doth call you to this, that he may pardon and bless you when you repent.</ns0:note>: for the meat-offering, and the drink-offering is withholden from the house of your God <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Vid. ver.</ns0:hi> 9. <ns0:hi>let.</ns0:hi> k. l. m. n.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 ¶ <ns0:note n="¶" place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>hap. 2.15.</ns0:note> Sanctifie ye <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">You Priests, Ministers of my God, set apart a day, or more dayes, appoint a time, forbid all servile work, and sensu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />al pleasures, do what you may to prepare for such a necessary work.</ns0:note> a fast <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Wherein to afflict your selves, confess your sins, re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pent of them, and sue out your pardon, return to God, that he may remove your present calamities, and prevent the future.</ns0:note>, call <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ev. 23.36.</ns0:note> a <ns0:note place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, day of <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> so<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lemn assembly <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Proclaim and publish it, that every one may know they are restrain'd from common, daily work, and that they are com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />manded to come together, most solemnly to seek the Lord.</ns0:note>, gather the elders <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Both for Age and for Authority, Magistrates and Rulers who possibly had been by their sins, more then others, cause of these grievous calamities, and should now be examples to others in repenting.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> all the inhabitants of the land <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Make this Fast as publick universal as you can, command all the people of the land, all that dwell with you, perhaps the Prophet intends Proselytes of the Law, and those of Commerce as well as the <ns0:hi>Iewes.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>into</ns0:hi> the house <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Courts of the Temple. for Priests only might go into the Temple it self, the Court of <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> where the people were wont to pray.</ns0:note> of the LORD your God <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Remember the Covenant by which you are his people, and he is your God<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> that you may plead his promises as well as wait for his mercies</ns0:note>, and cry unto the LORD <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">With tears of Repentance, with Prayer of Faith, cry more with the broken heart then loud voice.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. 30.7.</ns0:note> Alas <ns0:note place="bottom">This verse and the three next may be lookt upon either as a particular declaration of the grounds of this Fast, or as a di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rection how to manage the Fast, a suggesting to the people what they should spread before the Lord, or else as the words of the Priests, bewailing the calamitous state of the Land,</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">It is a very pathetical bemoaning themselves, which speaks their sense of the evil they suffer'd,</ns0:note> for the day <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">The day of trouble, sorrow and great distress.</ns0:note>: for <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. 13.6.</ns0:note> the day of the LORD <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">This explains the former; It is a day of greater troubles then yet they felt, troubles which God will heap upon them, a day in which God will be Judge, and pu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nish by the locusts, by the drought, and by <ns0:hi>Babylonians,</ns0:hi> unless you repent.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> at hand <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Great calamities were now upon them, and greater were approaching to them, if the Prophet <ns0:hi>Ioel</ns0:hi> aim at the Captivity either, of the two Tribes, it was 180 years off, if of the ten Tribes it was about 60 years off, for he Prophesi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth about the latter end of <ns0:hi>Ieroboam</ns0:hi> the second; it is likely therefore he aimeth at some other calamities.</ns0:note>, and as a destruction <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">A total over<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />throw of the Kingdom, the worship of God, and all your la<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bours in your land.</ns0:note> from the Almighty <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Whose displeasure as a consuming fire, can and will burn up all before it, his power and hand will do it, and then nothing can resist it.</ns0:note> shall it come <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Most certainly and speedi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly nothing can retard, or divert it, unless Fasting, Prayers and Tears, and amendment do it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 Is not the meat <ns0:note n="†" place="bottom">The question does most vehemently affirm our food, what we should eat, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> all provision we should live upon·</ns0:note> cut off <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Devoured by locusts, or withered with drought, 'tis perisht·</ns0:note> before our eyes <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">We see it, 'tis not so far off as what is foretold, 'tis under our eye.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>yea,</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Deut. 16.11.14, 15.</ns0:note> joy and gladness from the house of our God <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Sacrifices fail much, and Priests have scarce enough to live upon, while free will Offerings, first Fruits and Tithes, amount to very little, not sufficient to feast the Sacrificers and Offerers, who on such occasion did use to rejoyce in the house of God.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 The <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>grains.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> seed <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Called so from the seeds-man's scattering it abroad when he soweth it, and in this place only so used, for ought I can ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />serve, and yet this use of it here is justified by all the following words; the grain which is sown for the seed against next spring.</ns0:note> is rotten <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Is putrified, grown musty and fruitless, nor is this word any where else used in Scripture.</ns0:note> under their clods <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">And Earth, from under which the seed covered should spring up, but now as unsound, rotten and fruitless seed is lost under it.</ns0:note>, the garners <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Or Storehouses, Treasu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ries of Corn, in which 'twas kept for future use,</ns0:note> are laid desolate <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Either run to ruin, because the owners discouraged with the barrenness of the seasons, would not repair them, this will intimate that this judgment lasted some years, and is better ground for it, than the four sorts of vermin repeated one after another, in <ns0:hi>verse</ns0:hi> 4. or else desolate, being pull'd down, and the materials employ<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed for other uses, till they may have Corn to keep in them.</ns0:note>, the barns <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">In which they lodged their unthreshed Corn.</ns0:note> are broken down <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Neglected, and without repair.</ns0:note>; for the corn is withered <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">There was no use of them, no Corn to be laid up, all withered, and therefore the Barns were not re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />garded.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 How do the beasts groan <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">So great was the penury and want of sustenance, that the beasts in the field pincht with hunger, groaned, made dismal noise for fodder and water, the first word, <ns0:hi>beasts,</ns0:hi> is general, and contains all sorts.</ns0:note>? the herds of cattel <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">The greater Cattel which go wandering about, and range over all places, yet can find no pasturage.</ns0:note> are perplexed, because they have no pa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stures; yea, the flocks of sheep <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Which led by Shepherds, might likely be supposed better se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cured, yet their Shepherds find no Pasture, and the sheep pine away, and starve. These things are mentioned, either as con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vincing men of their stupidity, who were less sensible of pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sent miseries then brute beasts were, or to provoke them to lay to heart the pressing calamities, or as arguments that he would pity and relieve innocent brutes, though he punisht sinful brutes.</ns0:note> are made de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />solate.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 O LORD <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Maker and preserver of these poor famisht Cattel.</ns0:note>, to thee will I cry <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther 'tis the Prophets Prayer he maketh, or a form prescribed for the Priests.</ns0:note>: for the fire <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">The immoderate heats, or else the scorching and blasting flashes of fire in the air, which in those hot Coun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tries are more frequent and more pernicious then in colder Cli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mates.</ns0:note> hath devoured the <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>habitations</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> pastures <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">The fruitful and pleasant places where Shepherds pitcht their Tents, and were use to feed their sheep, all are parcht and dryed as if burnt with fire.</ns0:note> of the wil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derness <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Either because the Shepherds chose to pitch their Tents far from Cities and Towns, or else, because in those vast Wildernesses there were some fruitful Pastures scattered up and down, some lower places of Springs and Water-courses.</ns0:note>, and the flame <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">The flashes of fire from the Clouds, or in the Air, without Thunder, or else Lightenings with Thunder.</ns0:note> hath burnt all the trees <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">That they neither afford their fruit, their shade, or their green boughs for brouse for the relief of man or beast. This extream desolation should affect them all, it doth shame the sinfully sensless among them, and it is a good argu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment to use with God, whose creatures they are as well as man.</ns0:note> of the field.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 The beasts <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Vid. verse</ns0:hi> 18. <ns0:hi>let</ns0:hi> x.</ns0:note> of the field <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 104.2<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                  </ns0:note> cry <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">The wilder sort, that rove about many miles seeking their livelyhood, find no sustenance, they look up to God, and cry to him, these creatures that can better shift for themselves, yet can make no good shift; they utter their complaints in their sad tones, they have a voice to cry, as well as an eye to look to God.</ns0:note> also unto thee <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Who only canst open thy hand, and fill them, learn ye brutish among men, look and cry to God; And again, have pity O God, many of thy sinless crea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tures perish without relief, hear them, though thou shouldst not hear men.</ns0:note>: for the rivers of waters are dryed up <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Most extream and tedious drought, which hath dryed up the Rivers themselves, there is no drink for the Cattle, they must perish without help, unless thou O God send a plentiful and fruitful rain.</ns0:note>, and the fire hath devoured the pastures of the wil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derness <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Vid. this explain'd above <ns0:hi>verse</ns0:hi> 19. <ns0:hi>let.</ns0:hi> c. d. e.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
